Stated Claim / Post Context:
18 million people living in poverty depend on underwater meadows for food and income - but these vital habitats are under threat

Seagrass meadows have a vital role in the fight against poverty.

Actual Article Body:
Share article

Print article

At least 18 million people living in poverty across the Indo-Pacific fish in seagrass meadows, while around 6.5 million rely on them as their only fishing grounds. For these communities, the underwater habitats are not simply part of the natural environment but a source of food and a means of earning a living.

But these important fishing grounds face growing pressure from coastal development, changes in land use and poor water quality. When seagrass meadows are damaged or lost, the consequences can extend beyond wildlife. The fish and other marine life they support may also be affected, putting food supplies and household incomes at risk.

Our latest research examines the scale of this dependence and how it relates to poverty. The findings highlight a question that conservation efforts need to address: what happens to people whose livelihoods depend on habitats that are under growing pressure?

Seagrasses are flowering plants that grow in shallow coastal waters. They form underwater meadows that support fish and other marine life. People can fish in these habitats using simple nets, traps and lines, or collect shellfish and other marine animals by hand. Unlike some other fishing grounds, seagrass meadows can often be reached without a boat or expensive equipment.

This level of accessibility can be particularly important for households with few resources or alternative ways to earn money. Yet seagrass conservation is often discussed in terms of protecting wildlife and storing carbon. We have known that these habitats support fisheries, but we have had much less understanding of how many people living in poverty rely on them.

To investigate this, we analysed data from nearly 2,000 households in more than 150 coastal communities across Cambodia, Indonesia, the Philippines, Sri Lanka and Tanzania.

We looked at household incomes, fishing activities and the habitats people used to catch fish and collect other marine resources. We then compared the livelihoods of households using different fishing grounds, including those living in poverty.

More than 80% of households in the communities we studied were involved in fishing, either to earn money, provide food or both. Households that relied entirely on seagrass fisheries earned around 23% less than those fishing in other habitats, even after we accounted for differences in household size.

To put this in perspective, if a household earns £7.50 per day, a 23% difference amounts to roughly £52 a month. For a family already struggling to afford food, healthcare or education, this is a substantial amount of money.

The dependence was especially striking among households living in extreme poverty. Almost half fished in seagrass as well as other habitats, while more than a 25% relied on seagrass alone. This does not mean that seagrass fishing causes poverty. Rather, accessible fishing grounds may be particularly important to people who cannot afford a boat or specialist equipment.

We then combined our household data with estimates of how many people live near seagrass meadows. Across the five countries we studied, we estimate that 10.8 million people living in poverty use seagrass for fishing. Around 5.4 million may rely on it as their only fishing habitat.

The stakes go beyond income. In separate research published earlier this year, we found that fish communities associated with seagrass could provide a wider range of essential nutrients than those associated with coral reefs. Although reefs supported more fish overall, seagrass fish communities had greater potential to supply several important nutrients together.

These include iron, which helps prevent anaemia, zinc, which supports children’s growth and immune systems, calcium, which is essential for health bones, and omega-3 fatty acids which support brain development. For families that cannot afford a varied diet, fish, even as a soup or broth, can provide several of these nutrients in a single meal. Losing access to seagrass could therefore not only mean losing income, but also a vital source of nutrition, especially for children and vulnerable family members.

These risks are important considerations because seagrass meadows face pressure globally. Research suggests that around 20% of surveyed seagrass meadow area in the Indo-Pacific has been lost over the past 70 to 90 years, with coastal development and declining water quality among the major threats identified.

Elsewhere in the Indo-Pacific, researchers documented an 84% decline in fish abundance following substantial seagrass loss. For coastal families that depend on these habitats, this means fewer fish available to catch, fewer income opportunities and less food.

Protecting these habitats, however, is not as simple as restricting fishing. Conservation measures that limit access to fishing grounds could harm communities if they depend on them for food or income and have few alternatives. At the same time, local fishers may have little control over other sources of damage, such as pollution from agriculture or development along the coast.

Read more:
      Human connections to seagrass meadows date back 180,000 years, study reveals

Conservation plans therefore need to consider both the health of seagrass meadows and the people who depend on them. Where restrictions on fishing are proposed, decision-makers should assess the probable effects on local incomes and food supplies. They should also consider whether realistic alternatives are available and address damage caused by pollution and coastal development, rather than placing the burden of conservation on fishing communities alone.

In the Philippines, local fishing communities are already helping manage marine reserves that protect seagrass meadows. Some approaches allow fishing and shellfish collection to continue while restricting more damaging activities or protecting smaller areas where marine life can recover.

In Indonesia, years of forest clearance had increased soil erosion, washing sediment into coastal waters and threatening seagrass meadows. In response, local governments, communities and organisations came together to plant more than 4,500 trees along riverbanks to reduce the amount of sediment entering the sea and protecting the seagrass fishing grounds that local families depend on.

Protecting seagrass will not solve coastal poverty on its own, however. But our findings show why conservation policies need to recognise the people who depend on these habitats. Safeguarding seagrass means protecting not only marine life but also an important source of food and income for millions of people.

NYC food pantries are now stocking pet food for struggling households

BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM If you’ve ever moved a bit of food off your own plate just so your dog could eat, too, then you know the feeling this program is trying to address. It’s a pretty common one in New York City right now. And most people who surrender a pet to […]
The post NYC food pantries are now stocking pet food for struggling households first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.

Actual Article Body:
A new solution in your inbox every day.

BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

If you’ve ever moved a bit of food off your own plate just so your dog could eat, too, then you know the feeling this program is trying to address. It’s a pretty common one in New York City right now. And most people who surrender a pet to a shelter aren’t doing it lightly. They do it as the very last resort, when they’ve truly run out of ways to make it work.

NYC has put $500,000 toward the problem. The city is funding 22 food pantries across all five boroughs to stock and distribute free pet food, with supplies expected to start arriving within about two weeks.

Cassandra, a Brooklyn resident, has a three-year-old Shih Tzu named Teddy, who she’s had since he was two months old. “Sometimes I have to sacrifice a little of my food that way he doesn’t go hungry, until I can get more food for him,” she said. At The Campaign Against Hunger in Brooklyn, pantry director Tamara Dawson has watched the same dynamic for years. “They bring their pets with them and are feeding them online because they have been without,” she said.

The organization already offers free pet food to clients, but the supply has always depended on chasing grants and donors. The city funding makes that a little less precarious.

St. John’s Bread and Life in Brooklyn received a $17,000 voucher through the initiative. Staff said demand has grown since many clients saw their SNAP benefits reduced, something that moved through the whole household budget, pets included.

“The affordability crisis affects every member of a family, including the pets we love,” said Mayor Zohran Mamdani. “No New Yorker should have to choose between feeding themselves and feeding their pets.”

Animal welfare groups have tracked the connection between financial hardship and shelter surrender for years. Getting pet food to families early is a pretty practical way to keep that from happening.

Here are all 22 participating locations:

– Part of the Solution: 2759 Webster Ave., 10458

– New York Common Pantry: 1290 Hoe Ave., 10459

– Community Help in Park Slope: 200 Fourth Ave., 11217

– Metropolitan Council on Jewish Poverty: 5361 Preston Court, 11234

– On the Go Relief: 2832 Fulton Street, 11207

– St. John’s Bread and Life Food Pantry: 795 Lexington Ave., 11221

– The Campaign Against Hunger: 2004 Fulton Street, 11233

– YMCA Community Market: 2980 West 29th Street, 11224

– Holy Apostles Soup Kitchen Pantry: 296 Ninth Ave., 10001

– New York Common Pantry: 8 East 109th Street, 10029

– St. Clemens Food Pantry: 423 West 46th Street, 10036

– The Father’s Heart Ministries: 543-545 East 11th Street, 10009

– The Lower Eastside Girls Club: 402 East 8th Street, 10009

– Trinity’s Services and Food for the Homeless: 602 East 9th Street, 10009

– Project Hospitality: 205 Canal Street, 10304

– Feeding with TLC: 309 St. Paul’s Ave., 10304

Call ahead if you’re not sure what to bring or whether your nearest location is stocked yet. And if someone you know could use this, it’s the kind of thing that’s good to pass along.

People living past 100 in one tiny village share 3 daily habits

National Geographic's potential blue zone in Sardinia's Bolotana has 10 centenarians among 2,262 residents, and their plant-based diet holds secrets.

Actual Article Body:
This material may not be published, broadcast, rewritten, or redistributed. ©2026 FOX News Network, LLC. All rights reserved. Quotes displayed in real-time or delayed by at least 15 minutes. Market data provided by Factset. Powered and implemented by FactSet Digital Solutions. Legal Statement. Mutual Fund and ETF data provided by LSEG.

Blue Zones Founder Dan Buettner explores why women in a small Italian village are reaching age 100 at remarkable rates, highlighting the importance of friendships, shared responsibilities and everyday movement.

National Geographic researchers believe they may have discovered a new "blue zone."

A blue zone is a geographic region where residents show unusually high rates of longevity and survival into old age. The newest blue zone candidate is a small village called Bolotana, located on the Italian island of Sardinia.

In a 2024 snapshot, 10 of the village's 2,262 residents were at least 100 years old, according to National Geographic — roughly 10 times the Sardinian average and 11 times the U.S. average.

PEOPLE WHO LIVE TO 100 HAVE 3 DRINKS IN COMMON, LONGEVITY EXPERT SAYS

A team of researchers, including Dan Buettner — founder of Blue Zones, a company focused on longevity, and a National Geographic Fellow — set out to investigate Bolotana’s exceptional lifespan.

The findings were published in Frontiers in Aging.

Bolotana’s hilly streets encourage residents to walk as part of their daily routines. (Marisa Montibeller)

Buettner highlighted three lifestyle habits that are common among Bolotana’s long-lived residents.

"Here, men are participating more, and that could explain why women are doing better."

The study did not establish that these habits directly cause longevity, but researchers are examining how the village’s environment and traditions may contribute to its unusually high survival rates.

"The international team of demographers, their population scientists … were able to examine the birth records, death records and baptismal records and see that this is probably the richest, most complete data on centenarians in the world," Buettner told Fox News Digital.

AMERICA'S LIFESPAN HAS DOUBLED SINCE 1776 — EXPERTS REVEAL WHAT CHANGED

"For those of us who want to make it into our 90s and 100s in full health, this place does it better than anyplace else in the world."

The strongest longevity advantage appeared among Bolotana’s women, who ranked second only to Hong Kong for life expectancy at age 70 and survival from age 70 to 100.

Bolotana, Sardinia, is home to ancient olive groves. (Marisa Montibeller)

The original Sardinian blue zone was identified in the late 1990s and formally described in research published around 2000. Located in the mountainous region roughly 68 miles from Bolotana, it is known for unusually strong male longevity, according to Buettner.

Although Bolotana remains partly pastoral, it is also an agricultural community. Buettner suggested that this may mean men spend more time at home helping with household responsibilities, potentially reducing the burden on women.

Dan Buettner, middle, is pictured with two centenarian women of Bolotana. (Marisa Montibeller)

"In the original blue zone in the highlands, the [women] worried about the finances and raising children and the leaky roof," he said. "They're all alone. Here, men are participating more, and that could explain why women are doing better, because they're only bearing half the stress load instead of almost all of it."

Buettner believes the village’s strong social connections may be one factor behind the women’s longevity, although the study did not establish a cause.

GEORGIA WOMAN CELEBRATES 112TH BIRTHDAY, REVEALS HER SECRET TO A LONG LIFE

"We see women gathering in the library, baking bread together, making sweets together and going to church together," he said. "So, you see a much more socially connected society among the women in Bolotana than in the other blue zones."

As in many parts of Italy, Bolotana has a strong Catholic tradition. Buettner said church attendance may provide residents with faith, social connection and a sense of belonging.

Bolotana church culture connects its residents to faith and to each other. (Marisa Montibeller)

"It’s a sense of community, but it's also people proactively understanding that sitting down with a friend and talking about your troubles and your day with somebody who cares about you is a much more powerful drug than a pharmaceutical," Buettner said.

"The human species has shown this over and over, and Bolotana is a perfect example."

Diet varies among blue zones, but Bolotana’s traditional fare is largely plant-based, with a focus on beans, vegetables, wheat, olives and olive oil, along with some cheese and meat.

DOCTOR'S 10 RULES FOR LIVING LONGER, CELEBRATING MORE BIRTHDAYS AND MAKING EXTRA YEARS COUNT

"About 90% of a centenarian's diet has been all plant-based," Buettner said. "Not protein, by the way. These aren't protein loaders. These are complex carbohydrate loaders."

Dan Buettner prepares a traditional minestrone with Anna Maria Filia in Bolotana. (Marisa Montibeller)

A Bolotanese breakfast might consist of a piece of bread or cheese with local olives and a cup of coffee. Lunch, the biggest meal of the day that starts in the early afternoon, is "almost always" a minestrone soup made with locally grown seasonal vegetables and lots of beans.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"Beans are the cornerstone of the longevity diet here," Buettner said. "Garbanzo beans, lentil beans, pinto beans, cannellini beans — these are really the all-star of the diet."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Traditionally, residents ate meat about five times per month, usually as a celebratory food.

In the highlands, people traditionally cooked with lard, Buettner said, while Bolotana residents use olive oil from ancient trees.

Giaccomo Nieddu maintains an ancient olive grove in Bolotana. The oil contains unusually high levels of odd-chain fatty acids, which researchers are studying for possible links to longevity. (Marisa Montibeller)

Researchers are studying whether the oil’s unusually high levels of odd-chain fatty acids could be relevant to longevity.

Bolotana residents are not deliberately pursuing longer lives, the longevity researcher noted. The region has little emphasis on gym culture or biohacking.

"These are real humans with an average set of genes," Buettner said. "These aren’t superhumans with superhuman discipline or better genes."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"They’re not chasing longevity," he added. "It is the product of their environment."

Because Bolotana’s streets are steep and residents rarely drive within town, they typically walk to shops, cafés, workplaces and friends’ homes, Buettner said.

"It’s this sort of unconscious walking that’s far more important for longevity than going to the gym."

Bolotana residents walk steep hills for everyday tasks and socialize regularly. (Marisa Montibeller)

Buettner said Bolotana is an example of how daily routines and surroundings can encourage movement without requiring residents to schedule formal exercise.

Residents of walkable American communities have a three- to five-year life-expectancy advantage over those in less-walkable areas, he said.

Centenarians Salvatore and Nina spend time socializing daily in Bolotana. (Marisa Montibeller)

"If we want a healthier America, we have to start thinking about shaping our neighborhoods and our cities so people can unconsciously move and not rely on heaping another obligation on their busy lives to remember to go to the gym," the expert said.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Most of the things that lead to Bolotana longevity are also pleasant and make the journey a joy," he added.

Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

Protecting seagrass will not solve coastal poverty on its own, however. But our findings show why conservation policies need to recognise the people who depend on these habitats. Safeguarding seagrass means protecting not only marine life but also an important source of food and income for millions of people.

NYC food pantries are now stocking pet food for struggling households

BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM If you’ve ever moved a bit of food off your own plate just so your dog could eat, too, then you know the feeling this program is trying to address. It’s a pretty common one in New York City right now. And most people who surrender a pet to […]

Actual Article Body:
A new solution in your inbox every day.

BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

If you’ve ever moved a bit of food off your own plate just so your dog could eat, too, then you know the feeling this program is trying to address. It’s a pretty common one in New York City right now. And most people who surrender a pet to a shelter aren’t doing it lightly. They do it as the very last resort, when they’ve truly run out of ways to make it work.

NYC has put $500,000 toward the problem. The city is funding 22 food pantries across all five boroughs to stock and distribute free pet food, with supplies expected to start arriving within about two weeks.

Cassandra, a Brooklyn resident, has a three-year-old Shih Tzu named Teddy, who she’s had since he was two months old. “Sometimes I have to sacrifice a little of my food that way he doesn’t go hungry, until I can get more food for him,” she said. At The Campaign Against Hunger in Brooklyn, pantry director Tamara Dawson has watched the same dynamic for years. “They bring their pets with them and are feeding them online because they have been without,” she said.

The organization already offers free pet food to clients, but the supply has always depended on chasing grants and donors. The city funding makes that a little less precarious.

St. John’s Bread and Life in Brooklyn received a $17,000 voucher through the initiative. Staff said demand has grown since many clients saw their SNAP benefits reduced, something that moved through the whole household budget, pets included.

“The affordability crisis affects every member of a family, including the pets we love,” said Mayor Zohran Mamdani. “No New Yorker should have to choose between feeding themselves and feeding their pets.”

Animal welfare groups have tracked the connection between financial hardship and shelter surrender for years. Getting pet food to families early is a pretty practical way to keep that from happening.

Call ahead if you’re not sure what to bring or whether your nearest location is stocked yet. And if someone you know could use this, it’s the kind of thing that’s good to pass along.

People living past 100 in one tiny village share 3 daily habits

National Geographic's potential blue zone in Sardinia's Bolotana has 10 centenarians among 2,262 residents, and their plant-based diet holds secrets.

Actual Article Body:

Blue Zones Founder Dan Buettner explores why women in a small Italian village are reaching age 100 at remarkable rates, highlighting the importance of friendships, shared responsibilities and everyday movement.

National Geographic researchers believe they may have discovered a new "blue zone."

A blue zone is a geographic region where residents show unusually high rates of longevity and survival into old age. The newest blue zone candidate is a small village called Bolotana, located on the Italian island of Sardinia.

In a 2024 snapshot, 10 of the village's 2,262 residents were at least 100 years old, according to National Geographic — roughly 10 times the Sardinian average and 11 times the U.S. average.

PEOPLE WHO LIVE TO 100 HAVE 3 DRINKS IN COMMON, LONGEVITY EXPERT SAYS

A team of researchers, including Dan Buettner — founder of Blue Zones, a company focused on longevity, and a National Geographic Fellow — set out to investigate Bolotana’s exceptional lifespan.

The findings were published in Frontiers in Aging.

Bolotana’s hilly streets encourage residents to walk as part of their daily routines. (Marisa Montibeller)

Buettner highlighted three lifestyle habits that are common among Bolotana’s long-lived residents.

"Here, men are participating more, and that could explain why women are doing better."

The study did not establish that these habits directly cause longevity, but researchers are examining how the village’s environment and traditions may contribute to its unusually high survival rates.

"The international team of demographers, their population scientists … were able to examine the birth records, death records and baptismal records and see that this is probably the richest, most complete data on centenarians in the world," Buettner told Fox News Digital.

AMERICA'S LIFESPAN HAS DOUBLED SINCE 1776 — EXPERTS REVEAL WHAT CHANGED

"For those of us who want to make it into our 90s and 100s in full health, this place does it better than anyplace else in the world."

The strongest longevity advantage appeared among Bolotana’s women, who ranked second only to Hong Kong for life expectancy at age 70 and survival from age 70 to 100.

Bolotana, Sardinia, is home to ancient olive groves. (Marisa Montibeller)

The original Sardinian blue zone was identified in the late 1990s and formally described in research published around 2000. Located in the mountainous region roughly 68 miles from Bolotana, it is known for unusually strong male longevity, according to Buettner.

Although Bolotana remains partly pastoral, it is also an agricultural community. Buettner suggested that this may mean men spend more time at home helping with household responsibilities, potentially reducing the burden on women.

Dan Buettner, middle, is pictured with two centenarian women of Bolotana. (Marisa Montibeller)

"In the original blue zone in the highlands, the [women] worried about the finances and raising children and the leaky roof," he said. "They're all alone. Here, men are participating more, and that could explain why women are doing better, because they're only bearing half the stress load instead of almost all of it."

Buettner believes the village’s strong social connections may be one factor behind the women’s longevity, although the study did not establish a cause.

GEORGIA WOMAN CELEBRATES 112TH BIRTHDAY, REVEALS HER SECRET TO A LONG LIFE

"We see women gathering in the library, baking bread together, making sweets together and going to church together," he said. "So, you see a much more socially connected society among the women in Bolotana than in the other blue zones."

As in many parts of Italy, Bolotana has a strong Catholic tradition. Buettner said church attendance may provide residents with faith, social connection and a sense of belonging.

Bolotana church culture connects its residents to faith and to each other. (Marisa Montibeller)

"It’s a sense of community, but it's also people proactively understanding that sitting down with a friend and talking about your troubles and your day with somebody who cares about you is a much more powerful drug than a pharmaceutical," Buettner said.

"The human species has shown this over and over, and Bolotana is a perfect example."

Diet varies among blue zones, but Bolotana’s traditional fare is largely plant-based, with a focus on beans, vegetables, wheat, olives and olive oil, along with some cheese and meat.

DOCTOR'S 10 RULES FOR LIVING LONGER, CELEBRATING MORE BIRTHDAYS AND MAKING EXTRA YEARS COUNT

"About 90% of a centenarian's diet has been all plant-based," Buettner said. "Not protein, by the way. These aren't protein loaders. These are complex carbohydrate loaders."

Dan Buettner prepares a traditional minestrone with Anna Maria Filia in Bolotana. (Marisa Montibeller)

A Bolotanese breakfast might consist of a piece of bread or cheese with local olives and a cup of coffee. Lunch, the biggest meal of the day that starts in the early afternoon, is "almost always" a minestrone soup made with locally grown seasonal vegetables and lots of beans.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"Beans are the cornerstone of the longevity diet here," Buettner said. "Garbanzo beans, lentil beans, pinto beans, cannellini beans — these are really the all-star of the diet."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Traditionally, residents ate meat about five times per month, usually as a celebratory food.

In the highlands, people traditionally cooked with lard, Buettner said, while Bolotana residents use olive oil from ancient trees.

Giaccomo Nieddu maintains an ancient olive grove in Bolotana. The oil contains unusually high levels of odd-chain fatty acids, which researchers are studying for possible links to longevity. (Marisa Montibeller)

Researchers are studying whether the oil’s unusually high levels of odd-chain fatty acids could be relevant to longevity.

Bolotana residents are not deliberately pursuing longer lives, the longevity researcher noted. The region has little emphasis on gym culture or biohacking.

"These are real humans with an average set of genes," Buettner said. "These aren’t superhumans with superhuman discipline or better genes."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"They’re not chasing longevity," he added. "It is the product of their environment."

Because Bolotana’s streets are steep and residents rarely drive within town, they typically walk to shops, cafés, workplaces and friends’ homes, Buettner said.

"It’s this sort of unconscious walking that’s far more important for longevity than going to the gym."

Bolotana residents walk steep hills for everyday tasks and socialize regularly. (Marisa Montibeller)

Buettner said Bolotana is an example of how daily routines and surroundings can encourage movement without requiring residents to schedule formal exercise.

Residents of walkable American communities have a three- to five-year life-expectancy advantage over those in less-walkable areas, he said.

Centenarians Salvatore and Nina spend time socializing daily in Bolotana. (Marisa Montibeller)

"If we want a healthier America, we have to start thinking about shaping our neighborhoods and our cities so people can unconsciously move and not rely on heaping another obligation on their busy lives to remember to go to the gym," the expert said.

"Most of the things that lead to Bolotana longevity are also pleasant and make the journey a joy," he added.

Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.
